records.section_heading: 7.2.b. The geological record in American Samoa
records.question: What migration rate of the centre of volcanism from Manua to Tutuila did McDougall (1985) derive?
ground_truth_chunks: When all the ages of shield-building volcanism in American Samoa are examined together, it is evident that the youngest volcanism occurred in the east (on Tau) and the oldest in the west (on Tutuila).
From the available dates, a rate of migration of the centre of volcanism from Manua to Tutuila of about 10 cm/year was derived by McDougall (1985).

records.question: According to Kear and Wood (1959), what is the probable age of the Salani Volcanics?
records.ground_truth_answer: Kear and Wood (1959) suggested a probable age for the Salani Volcanics of the Last Interglacial (~125 000 BP).
ground_truth_chunks: The Salani Volcanics were erupted in both main islands following a period of quiescence after the end of Fagaloa/Vanu volcanism.
The degree of weathering of the lavas suggested to Kear and Wood (1959) a probable age for this activity of Last Interglacial (~125 000 BP).

records.section_heading: 7.3.a. Recent land/sea-level changes in American Samoa
records.question: What are the average elevations of the three levels of emergence on Tutuila reported in this section?
records.ground_truth_answer: The three levels average approximately 3.9 m (high-level), 1.55 m (second/lower level), and 0.25 m (lowest level).
ground_truth_chunks: This level of emergence averages 3.9 m and is represented by a large piece of emerged reef in Vatia Bay (Plate 7.1).
A second, lower level of emergence ranges from 0.87 to 2.4 m and averages 1.55 m.
The lowest level of emergence is represented by emerged reef 0.06-0.39 m (average 0.25 m) and is confined to the north coast of Tutuila.

records.section_heading: 7.3.b. Recent land/sea-level changes on Upolu, Western Samoa
records.question: What emergence levels did Kear and Wood (1959) identify on Upolu, and with which deposits were they associated?
records.ground_truth_answer: Kear and Wood (1959) identified sedimentary evidence of emergence at 1.5–2.4 m (associated with the Tafagamanu Sand), 4.6 m (associated with the Nuutele Sand) and 9 m (associated with the Vini Tuff).
ground_truth_chunks: In their 1959 account of the geology of Western Samoa, Kear and Wood found sedimentary evidence of emergence at 1.5-2.4 m (Tafagamanu Sand), 4.6 m (Nuutele Sand) and 9 m (Vini Tuff). The latter two levels are found almost exclusively on the smaller islands in Western Samoa.

Kear and Wood (1959) regarded shore platforms 1.8-2.4 m above sea level on the coast east of Apia as coeval with the Tafagamanu Sand level, which they regarded as being formed at a higher sea level, dated at the type site to 1180±55 BP (Grant-Taylor and Rafter 1962).

records.question: What elevations of emerged shorelines have been reported on Uvéa (Wallis) Island?
records.ground_truth_answer: Emerged shorelines have been reported at 7.6 m and 1.7 m.
ground_truth_chunks: Evidence of emergence similar to that in Samoa exists on Uvéa (Stearns 1945).
There are emerged shorelines at 7.6 m and 1.7 m which are largely erosional in character but also include patches of emerged reef and 'marine conglomeratic limestone'.

records.question: What rate of movement of the lithosphere over the hotspot is indicated by the best-fitting regression line?
ground_truth_chunks: When these ages are plotted (Figure 7.7), the best-fitting regression line yields a rate of movement of the lithosphere over a fixed hotspot some 150 km east of Tau of 7.69 cm/year.
This figure is within Duncan's (1985) estimate of 7.7±2.5 cm/year for the age-progressive trend along the Samoa island-seamount chain.
